content: Hypertrophic and keloid scars are skin conditions that arise from abnormal wound healing processes. These scars can cause significant physical symptoms such as itching and pain, as well as psychological distress, negatively impacting patients' quality of life. Various treatment modalities are employed to manage these scars, including intralesional corticosteroids, surgical interventions, and, more recently, laser therapy. However, laser therapy is costly and may lead to adverse effects, necessitating a thorough evaluation of its benefits and risks. The objective of this study was to assess the effects of laser therapy in treating hypertrophic and keloid scars. A comprehensive search was conducted in March 2021 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and LILACS. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant studies, with no restrictions on language, publication date, or study setting. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing laser therapy with placebo, no treatment, or other interventions were included. Fifteen RCTs involving 604 participants (children and adults) were included in the analysis. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 10 to 120 participants, with a mean of 40.27 participants per study. In cases where different parts of the same scar were randomized, each scar segment was treated as a unit of analysis, resulting in 906 scar segments. The follow-up periods for participants varied between 12 weeks and 12 months. All included studies were found to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain, particularly due to the lack of blinding of participants and personnel. The variability in intervention types, control groups, follow-up durations, and limitations in reported data restricted the ability to pool data for comparisons. Several secondary outcomes, such as cosmesis, treatment tolerance, patient preference, adherence, and quality of life changes, were not reported in any of the included studies. When comparing laser therapy to no treatment, low-certainty evidence suggested that 585-nm pulsed-dye laser (PDL) might improve hypertrophic and keloid scars, making them less severe (risk ratio [RR] 1.96; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.11 to 3.45; two studies, 60 scar segments). However, the effects of non-ablative fractional laser (NAFL) and fractional carbon dioxide (CO2) laser on hypertrophic and keloid scar severity remain unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Eight studies reported treatment-related adverse effects, but insufficient data were available for further analysis. When comparing laser therapy to other treatments, the evidence was very uncertain. For example, it is unclear whether 585-nm PDL is more effective than intralesional corticosteroid triamcinolone acetonide (TAC), intralesional fluorouracil (5-FU), or a combination of TAC and 5-FU. Similarly, the effects of erbium laser compared to TAC on hypertrophic scar severity are uncertain. Other comparisons, such as 585-nm PDL versus silicone gel sheeting, fractional CO2 laser versus TAC, and fractional CO2 laser versus verapamil, lacked sufficient data to draw conclusions about scar severity. Adverse effects associated with laser therapy, including pain, skin charring, telangiectasia, skin atrophy, purpuric discolorations, hypopigmentation, and erosion, were reported with very low-certainty evidence, preventing meaningful comparisons between treatments. When laser therapy was combined with other treatments, the evidence remained very uncertain. For instance, it is unclear whether 585-nm PDL combined with TAC and 5-FU leads to better outcomes than TAC and 5-FU alone. Similarly, the effects of CO2 laser combined with TAC compared to cryosurgery plus TAC, or neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser combined with intralesional corticosteroid diprospan and 5-FU compared to diprospan and 5-FU alone, are uncertain. The impact of helium-neon (He-Ne) laser combined with specific silicone-based creams compared to the creams alone is also unclear. Adverse effects such as pain, skin atrophy, erythema, telangiectasia, hypopigmentation, regrowth, hyperpigmentation, and depigmentation were reported with very low-certainty evidence, making it impossible to draw conclusions about the comparative safety of these treatments. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to definitively support or refute the effectiveness of laser therapy for treating hypertrophic and keloid scars. The available data are also inadequate to perform a detailed analysis of treatment-related adverse effects. The heterogeneity of the studies, conflicting results, design limitations, and small sample sizes highlight the need for high-quality trials. Future studies should use validated scales and core outcome sets, consider patients' perspectives and values, include long-term follow-up, and report recurrence rates to determine whether laser therapy offers superior outcomes compared to other treatments for hypertrophic and keloid scars.
